```{r, include=FALSE}

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 8,

  echo = TRUE,
  warning = TRUE,
  message = TRUE

```

We start by bringing in the tagbio library.  If you don't have this installed, please do so now:

```
library(remotes)
install_bitbucket("cloudfolks/tagbio", ref = "master", subdir = "tagbio")
```

Once installed, load the library.

```{r}
library(tagbio)
```

Next, we connect to a remote tagbio server.  You'll need to get an API key if you don't have one yet from the tag.bio profile page (for example: [https://demo.tag.bio/profile](https://demo.tag.bio/profile) ).  The API key can be supplied as a parameter to the call, saved in a system parameter called `TAGBIO_API_KEY` or placed in a file called `.tagbio.json` in your `HOME` directory.

```{r}
tag_con <- tagConnect(host_url = "https://demo.tag.bio",
                      api_key = "<API_KEY>")
```

To see what data products are available on the remote server, we use the `summary` method.

```{r}
summary(tag_con)
```

The `key` column in the table lists the data product names.  We can access a data product this way:


```{r}
fc <- tbl(tag_con, "fc-catalyze")
```


Let's look at what data collections are available for this data product.  Think of data collection as columns in a data frame.

```{r}
summary(fc)
```

Finally, let's grab data from the data product and lod into a tibble.  You can use familiar select/filter commands that should feel familiar.  The `collect` call initiates the download.

```{r}
# pull unique patient-cancer list from data product
patients_per_cancer <- fc |>
  select(`Patient ID`, `Cancer Subtype`) |>
  collect() |>
  filter(!is.na(`Cancer Subtype` != "NA")) |>
  distinct()
```
